q: A Card must accept as children some text, a number, several elements, or nothing at all. Which type should its children prop have?
options: ReactElement
ReactNode
JSX.Element
string | ReactElement[]
explain: ReactNode is the union of everything React can render: elements, strings, numbers, booleans, null, undefined and iterables of nodes. ReactElement is the tempting answer, but it accepts only JSX elements: text fails with TS2747 and a number with TS2322.

q: What does ComponentPropsWithoutRef<'button'> give the shop's Button?
options: Only the event handlers of a native button, such as onClick and onFocus
The props of the Button component itself, read from its definition
Every native <button> prop except ref
Every native button prop, with each one made required
explain: It is the full set of native button props (handlers, disabled, type, aria-*), so the component can intersect it with its own props and spread the rest onto the element. Only the "WithoutRef" part removes something: ref, which ComponentProps<'button'> includes (measured with @types/react 19.3.0).

q: With the React 19 types, what is the type of inputRef after const inputRef = useRef<HTMLInputElement>(null)?
options: RefObject<HTMLInputElement | null>: check current before use
MutableRefObject<HTMLInputElement>, so current is never null
RefObject<HTMLInputElement>, whose current React sets before the first render runs
Ref<HTMLInputElement>, which cannot be read directly
explain: Measured: the assignment to RefObject<HTMLInputElement | null> compiles, and inputRef.current.focus() fails with TS18047 ("possibly null"). current really is null until React attaches the element, and the types say so; inputRef.current?.focus() is the fix.

q: In React 19, how should the shared SearchField let the order search form focus its input?
options: Wrap it in forwardRef, which React 19 requires for any ref
Expose a focus() method through a context
Pass the ref under another name, such as inputRef, because ref is reserved
Declare a ref prop typed Ref<HTMLInputElement> and pass it on
explain: Since React 19, a function component receives ref as an ordinary prop, and react.dev says forwardRef is no longer necessary and will be deprecated. forwardRef still works, which makes it tempting, but new components do not need it, and renaming the prop was a workaround from before React 19.

q: Why does the team replace { isLoading: boolean; isError: boolean; error?: Error; data?: OrderSummary[] } with a union on status?
options: A union renders faster, because React compares a single status field instead of four separate flags
Each state holds only its own fields, so impossible combinations cannot be written
Booleans are not allowed in props under strict mode
The union lets the component skip the error state entirely
explain: Four independent fields allow 16 shapes, such as loading and error at once; the union allows exactly three, and inside if (state.status === 'success') the compiler knows data exists. Performance is not the reason: types are erased before React ever runs.

q: In LinkActionProps, what is the job of onClick?: never?
options: It makes the link's click handler optional
It strips onClick from the rendered <a> at runtime, so the handler never fires
It makes onClick together with href a compile error
It tells React to ignore click events on links
explain: No value has type never, so the link member accepts onClick only when it is absent; with href and onClick together, no member matches and tsc reports TS2322. Types have no effect at runtime, which rules out the second option.

q: The orders screen renders <DataTable rows={orders} getRowKey={…} columns={[…]} /> with no type argument. Where does Row come from?
options: It is inferred from rows, and the columns are checked against it
It defaults to any, because no type argument was written at the call site
It defaults to unknown, so render must narrow each row
It is read from the key of the first column
explain: TypeScript infers a component's type parameters from its props, like any function call; rows={orders} makes Row the order type. That is why { key: 'total' } fails with TS2322 once the field is totalCents. Nothing falls back to any, which is precisely what the old table did.

q: What is the main cost of the polymorphic Text with an as prop, as measured in the lesson?
options: It renders an extra wrapper around the chosen element, which breaks CSS selectors
It cannot accept children
It only works with HTML tags, not with components
Unreadable errors, an unchecked implementation, slower type-checking
explain: Inside, the element is a plain ElementType; the errors dump nested Omit types; and 200 uses added about 9,200 instantiations against 21 for a plain button (tsc 6.0.3). It renders exactly one element and accepts components such as a router Link as well as tags.

q: Why does the cart context use createContext<CartContextValue | null>(null) with a useCart hook that throws on null?
options: Because createContext requires null as its default whenever the value is an object
A missing provider fails loudly, and callers get a non-null value
Because use cannot read a context whose default is an object
It makes the context cheaper to re-render
explain: The throw turns a missing provider into an error with a clear message (measured: "useCart must be used inside <CartProvider>"), and the check removes null from the returned type. A fake default object would compile too, which is why it is tempting, but it hides the missing provider, as the empty cart did.

q: With exactOptionalPropertyTypes on, which value is a valid OrderPatch = Partial<Pick<OrderDetail, 'shippingAddress' | 'deliveryNote'>>, where deliveryNote: string | null?
options: { deliveryNote: undefined }
{ status: 'refunded' }
{ deliveryNote: null }
{ deliveryNote: 42 }
explain: null is part of the field's type, so it compiles, and the API reads it as "clear the note". undefined looks harmless, but under exactOptionalPropertyTypes an optional key means "absent", not "set to undefined", and tsc rejects it with TS2375. status is not picked (TS2353).

q: The badge map is declared { … } as const satisfies Record<OrderStatus, BadgeStyle>. A developer adds the status cancelled to OrderStatus. What happens?
options: The map fails to compile until it has a cancelled entry
The badge for cancelled falls back to the first entry
Nothing at compile time; the badge shows undefined at runtime
The map compiles, but statusBadges.paid.icon widens to string
explain: Record<OrderStatus, …> requires one key per status, and satisfies checks the object against it: measured, a missing key fails with TS1360 in tsc 6.0.3 (TS2741 in 7.0.2). Literal types are kept by as const, so paid.icon stays 'check'.

q: In the old fetcher, const body = await response.json(); body.anything.goes; compiled. Why?
options: response.json() returns Promise<unknown>, and unknown allows property access
TypeScript skips type checking inside async functions
The fetch types infer the body type from the URL
json() returns Promise<any> in the DOM types, which turns checks off
explain: The DOM types declare json() as returning Promise<any>, and everything read from an any is any too. unknown is the opposite: reading a property on it fails until you narrow or parse, which is why the fixed fetcher writes const body: unknown.

q: What does tsc report for the last line?
options: Nothing: a string is a valid React element
TS2747: IconSlot does not accept text as a child
TS2322 on the return statement: a component cannot return its children prop directly
TS2503: ReactElement is not exported by the React 19 types
explain: Measured with @types/react 19.3.0: "'IconSlot' components don't accept text as child elements" (TS2747). A string is a valid ReactNode, not a ReactElement, which is the confusion behind the first option. Returning children is fine because a ReactElement is a valid return value.

q: After upgrading the storefront to the React 19 types, const emptyState: JSX.Element = <p>No orders yet</p>; fails with TS2503. Which fix would you ship?
options: Add "jsx": "preserve" to tsconfig.json
Type it as any until the React types are fixed upstream in DefinitelyTyped
Import JSX from react, or let TypeScript infer the type
Downgrade @types/react to the previous major version
explain: The React 19 types no longer declare a global JSX namespace, hence "Cannot find namespace 'JSX'"; importing it from react compiles (measured), and most of the time the annotation is not needed at all. The jsx option controls how JSX is emitted, not where the namespace comes from.

q: Which line fails to compile, and why?
options: The last line (TS18048): isLoading does not rule out a pending query that is not fetching
error.message: the error is typed unknown by default
The destructuring line: a discriminated union loses its narrowing as soon as it is destructured
None: after both checks, data is always defined
explain: Measured with TanStack Query 5.104.5: "'data' is possibly 'undefined'" (TS18048) on the last line. The reference defines isLoading as isFetching && isPending, so a disabled query passes both checks; early returns on isPending and isError compile, destructured or not. The default error type is Error, not unknown.

q: An interviewer asks you to type the state of a "refund order" request in the back office (not started, running, failed with a message, done with a refund id). Which design would you defend?
options: { isRunning: boolean; isDone: boolean; error?: string; refundId?: string }
A string enum RefundState plus a separate refundId variable
{ state: string; payload: any }, so new states need no type change
A union on status: idle, running, failed with message, done with refundId
explain: The union puts each field in the only state where it exists, so refundId can be read only after checking status === 'done', and adding a state is caught by the exhaustiveness check from M04. The flags look simpler but allow running and done at once, and any gives up checking.

q: A colleague types the shared action as below. What happens on the last line?
options: TS2322: the object matches neither member
It compiles: excess property checks accept a key of any member
TS2353: onClick does not exist on LinkProps
It compiles, and Action calls refundOrder when the agent clicks the rendered link
explain: Measured: no error. On a union, the excess property check accepts any key that exists in some member, so the call is assignable to LinkProps; the component then renders a link and silently drops the handler. Adding onClick?: never to LinkProps and href?: never to ClickProps turns it into TS2322.

q: This line, in status-pill.tsx, breaks the build with TS17008. What is the bug?
code: export const StatusPill = (props: { value: T; format: (value: T) => string }) => {props.format(props.value)};
options: Arrow functions cannot be generic in TypeScript
A component can only have a type parameter when it is declared with React.FC<Props>
In .tsx, <T> parses as a JSX tag: write <T,> or a function
T needs a constraint such as T extends object
explain: Measured: "JSX element 'T' has no corresponding closing tag" (TS17008), a parse error, not a type error. <T,> or a function declaration removes the ambiguity. Generic arrows are fine in .ts files, and React.FC makes generics harder, not possible.

q: The refund dialog renders <Select options={refundReasons} value="broken" onChange={trackReason} getLabel={…} />, where refundReasons is ['damaged', 'late_delivery', 'wrong_item'] as const and trackReason accepts any string. It compiles. Which change makes it fail?
options: Type value as NoInfer<Option> in SelectProps
Remove as const from refundReasons
Add Option extends string as a constraint
Type options as Option[] instead of readonly Option[]
explain: Without NoInfer, TypeScript collects candidates from value too and widens Option to include "broken"; with it, only options decides and the call fails with TS2322 (both measured). A string constraint still accepts "broken", and removing as const widens Option to string, the opposite of the goal.

q: A teammate proposes an as prop on every component of @shop/ui, buttons and dialogs included, "for flexibility". What is the senior answer?
options: Agree: once the types compile, polymorphism costs nothing to the team or to the compiler
Agree, but write the props with any to keep compile times low
Refuse all polymorphism and wrap native elements by hand in every app
Keep as for a few primitives; use separate components elsewhere
explain: The cost is real and measured: unreadable errors, an unchecked implementation, and about 9,200 instantiations for 200 uses. Primitives earn it; a button that becomes a link changes behaviour, so separate components (or Radix asChild, Base UI render) are clearer. Refusing everything is the over-correction.

q: What does tsc report on the last line?
options: Nothing: TypeScript infers the tuple [boolean, () => void] from the array literal
TS2349: the inferred type is an array, so toggleCart may be a boolean
TS2554: useDisclosure expects one argument
TS2304: toggleCart is not defined
explain: An array literal is inferred as an array of the union of its elements, not as a tuple. Measured: TS2349 ("Not all constituents … are callable"), plus TS2722 under noUncheckedIndexedAccess. return [isOpen, toggle] as const gives readonly [boolean, () => void]. The argument has a default value, so the call with none is valid.

q: Why does setOrders([order]) fail with TS2322 here, and what is the fix?
options: It is inferred as never[]; write useState<OrderSummary[]>([])
State arrays are read-only; use orders.push(order) instead
setOrders only accepts a function; write setOrders(() => [order])
The state is any[], which strict mode refuses; add as OrderSummary[] to the call
explain: With nothing to infer from, an empty array literal gives never[] under strict settings, and measured, "Type 'OrderSummary' is not assignable to type 'never'" (TS2322). A type argument states the intent. Mutating with push would compile against a typed array, but React would not re-render.

q: What does tsc report for the first export?
options: Nothing: Omit removes id from each member and keeps the other fields
TS2322: status must be 'paid' | 'refunded'
TS2353: Omit on a union keeps only shared keys
TS2741: refundedAt is missing
explain: Omit is a mapped type over keyof OrderView, and the keys of a union are those its members share: here only status (measured: the second export compiles, and paidAt fails with TS2353). A distributive version, T extends unknown ? Omit<T, K> : never, applies Omit to each member.

q: Asked to "write a pick that keeps key safety", which signature would you ship?
options: function pick<T>(source: T, keys: string[]): Partial<T>
function pick<T extends object, K extends keyof T>(source: T, keys: readonly K[]): Pick<T, K>
function pick(source: object, keys: string[]): Record<string, unknown>
function pick<T, K extends string>(source: T, keys: K[]): Record<K, unknown>
explain: K extends keyof T rejects unknown keys (measured: 'total' fails with TS2322), and the Pick<T, K> return type knows exactly which keys exist (.totalCents fails with TS2339). Partial<T> looks close, but it accepts any string key and returns every field as optional.

q: What is the type Statuses?
options: string
never, because a readonly tuple is not an array
readonly ['paid', 'shipped']
'paid' | 'shipped'
explain: The tuple matches readonly (infer Item)[], and infer captures the element type, the union of its literal members (measured: assigning 'refunded' fails with TS2322). It would be never without readonly in the pattern, because a readonly tuple does not match a mutable array type. as const keeps the literals, so it is not string.

q: Which call fails to compile with the lesson's buildPath and RouteParams?
options: buildPath('/orders/:orderId', { orderId: 'ord_7f3k' })
buildPath('/orders', {})
buildPath('/orders/:orderId/refunds/:refundId', { orderId: 'ord_7f3k' })
buildPath('/orders/:orderId/refunds/:refundId', { orderId: 'ord_7f3k', refundId: 'ref_2b' })
explain: The conditional type extracts both orderId and refundId from the pattern, so an object without refundId fails (TS2345 in tsc 6.0.3, TS2741 in 7.0.2, both measured). A pattern with no parameter yields {}, so buildPath('/orders', {}) compiles.

q: The badge map must have one entry per OrderStatus, and statusBadges.paid.icon must keep the type 'check'. Which declaration does both?
options: const statusBadges = { … } as const satisfies Record<OrderStatus, BadgeStyle>
const statusBadges: Readonly<Record<OrderStatus, BadgeStyle>> = { … } as const
const statusBadges = { … } as Record<OrderStatus, BadgeStyle>
const statusBadges = { … } as const
explain: satisfies checks every key and value against the record without changing the variable's type, and as const keeps the literals. The annotated version also checks the keys, which makes it tempting, but the annotation, not as const, decides the variable's type: measured, paid.icon widens to the whole icon union (TS2322 against 'check'). as even accepted an object with three statuses missing, and as const alone checks nothing.

q: Which fix for Monday's NaN € incident would you ship?
options: Write useQuery<Order[]>(…) so that the data is typed at every call site of the hook
Replace as Order[] with as unknown as Order[], which is stricter
Parse the body as unknown with a schema in fetchOrders
Rename the field back to total in the BFF and add a comment
explain: Only a runtime check can catch a payload that changed after the build; measured with Zod 4.6.7, the old body fails at path ["items", 0, "totalCents"]. A type argument on useQuery is the same unchecked claim as as, moved elsewhere, and as unknown as is looser, not stricter.

q: In code review you see const order = 5 as Order; fail with TS2352, and the author "fixes" it with 5 as unknown as Order. What do you say?
options: Approve: the double cast is the documented way to convert types
Ask for a real fix: the double cast silences the only check
Approve, but ask for satisfies Order on the next line
Ask for <Order>5, the angle-bracket cast, which TypeScript checks more strictly than as
explain: as refuses only conversions with no overlap (TS2352, measured); going through unknown removes even that, and the program still holds a number where an Order is expected. Angle-bracket casts are the same assertion with another syntax, and they do not parse in .tsx files.

q: An interviewer asks: "Enum or literal union for the order statuses in the back office?" Which answer fits the lesson?
options: An enum, because only enums give named constants
An enum, because a union cannot be iterated at runtime
Either one: since TypeScript 5, both compile to the same JavaScript object at runtime
A literal union, plus an as const object when runtime values are needed
explain: Measured: a string enum fails under erasableSyntaxOnly (TS1294), and label('paid') fails with TS2345 when the parameter is the enum. An as const object gives named constants and an iterable list, which covers the two reasons people pick enums. They do not compile to the same JavaScript: a union emits nothing, an enum emits an object.
